item.title: Lumbar Quadratus Lumborum — Positional Ease
clinicalUse: A person feels a familiar localized ache when rising from a chair or reaching to one side. The question is whether a specific quadratus-lumborum-related tender point can be made comfortably quieter in a shortened position.
Consider only after assessment of mechanical versus non-musculoskeletal pain, neurological features and irritability; a tender point is not a definitive diagnosis.
The movement you will retest is standing side-bending or another familiar, comfortable functional task.
patientPosition: Begin in supported side-lying or another relaxed position where the lumbar region and pelvis can be moved as one comfortable unit.
Use pillows under the waist, knees and head. The treated side must be able to move toward comfortable shortening rather than hanging in an uncontrolled stretch.
therapistPosition: Stand beside the trunk with a secure stance, one hand supporting the pelvis and the other monitoring the relevant tender area as appropriate.
Keep the patient's legs supported and do not rely on forceful twisting to create an apparent position of ease.
stabilization: Support the rib cage and pelvis; control their relationship without forced rotation.
If the tender point becomes more sensitive, undo the latest adjustment. The patient's feedback is your compass.
contact: Palpate the relevant quadratus lumborum region with light, respectful contact, avoiding the kidney area and unnecessary deep abdominal or flank pressure.
Use a supported hand to monitor relative tenderness; the positioning hand gently controls pelvic hike or side-bending, not high-velocity manipulation.
forceDirection: Gently approximate the iliac crest toward the ipsilateral lower ribs through comfortable trunk side-bending and/or pelvic hiking on the treated side, adjusting until tenderness is reduced.
The preferred position is the one that feels easier to this patient, not a fixed posture forced to match a diagram.
dosage: For a selected classical SCS-style protocol, a comfortable hold around 60–90 seconds may be used by trained clinicians; it is a protocol convention, not a guaranteed optimum.
Return to neutral very slowly, then reassess rather than immediately adding more positioning force.
steps: Record the patient's familiar standing side-bend or sit-to-stand discomfort before treatment.
Exclude red flags and clarify that a local tender point does not explain all causes of back pain.
Position side-lying with comfortable pillows, locate the clinically relevant tender area with gentle monitoring pressure.
Bring the tissues toward ease by controlled ipsilateral side-bending and/or pelvic approximation; do not force rotation.
Fine-tune until the tender point is notably less sensitive and the patient feels relaxed; abandon any painful position.
Maintain the comfortable protocol hold, then guide the trunk and pelvis back to neutral slowly.
Repeat the original movement and add graded active trunk control if the response is helpful.
reassess: Comfort during the same side-bend or sit-to-stand task
Reported tenderness at the original point under comparable light contact
Symptoms and activity tolerance over subsequent movement
mistakes: Mistaking painful lumbar rotation for adequate shortening: comfortable positioning is the point of this method.
Pressing hard into the flank to 'prove' a tender point exists.
Promising that one hold realigned vertebrae or permanently corrected fascial structure.
safety: Stop for new neurological symptoms, severe unrelenting pain, suspected fracture or other red flags; refer as clinically indicated.
Avoid direct aggressive pressure over the renal/flank region and avoid positions that stress an unstable spine or recent surgery.
Do not proceed when a position of ease cannot be found without discomfort.
item.visualCue: Softly approximate same-side rib and iliac crest → monitor ease → slow return → retest familiar side-bend.

story.title: The chair that suddenly became a challenge
story.scene: A graphic designer rises from a chair and rubs one side of the low back. 'The chair used to be my friend.' Side-bending reproduces a familiar localized ache, but the clinician first checks whether this is really a reasonable muscle-focused presentation.
story.clinicalDecision: Instead of making the already sensitive area stretch more, the therapist supports the pelvis and gently approximates the same-side rib and iliac crest until the monitored tender region feels easier. The position is adjusted to comfort, not to match a dramatic photo.
story.retest: The patient stands and repeats the same side-bend. If it feels easier, that gives the clinician a useful short-term clue. The next chapter belongs to active movement, not to the claim that a bone moved back into place.
story.punchline: The chair is not the villain. Our first guess might be.
story.evidenceCaveat: Evidence for positional release in low-back pain is very uncertain. A 2025 synthesis found very-low-certainty support mainly when combined with other care; it does not validate this exact QL protocol.
